title: The August 1943 Uprising in Białystok
summary: The uprising stands at the center of the community’s story of organized resistance during the destruction of Bialystok Jewry.
editorialContent:
![Białystok, the city whose ghetto was the setting of the uprising](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg/1920px-Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A revolt prepared in the shadow of liquidation

The Białystok ghetto uprising was not a bid to defeat the German forces surrounding the city. Its fighters faced a far stronger enemy and scant weapons. Their immediate hopes were to resist the ghetto’s destruction, open a way out for others, and—if they could—escape to the forests and join partisan groups. The revolt became a lasting symbol not because it succeeded militarily, but because the community remembered the decision to fight when the Germans were carrying out mass deportations.

The memorial book’s accounts place the main uprising on **16 August 1943**, when German forces entered the ghetto to liquidate it. Several supplied records repeat that date: one calls it the uprising’s beginning; another associates it with Lyube Subatnik’s death; and another describes vehicles and perpetrators entering the ghetto that day. The records also preserve a conflicting reference to an uprising on 6 August and an OCR-derived entry giving 16 August 1942. Those references do not match the other accounts of the final liquidation. They should not be silently merged with them: the wider historical record also dates the uprising to 16 August 1943. The event is linked in the book’s records with [the Białystok ghetto uprising](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_116b6268374ccc013aa7032a), [the August 16 uprising](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_66820a88d1b6fb044867fe65), and [the August 1943 operation](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_a9d5642f92750cf1ce4f234b).

The broader record explains why resistance had been prepared in advance. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the ghetto as holding Jews from Białystok and the surrounding region, many of them forced to work in factories. After a mass deportation in February 1943, the August operation threatened the community that remained. The museum’s account identifies the underground’s objective as breaking out and reaching partisans, and places the fighting near Smolna Street. ([USHMM, “Bialystok”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok))

## Organization and the choices behind resistance

The memorial book recalls preparations made under the constant threat of a new “aktion.” Underground organizers built shelters, posted guards, planned sabotage in the factories, and tried to maintain contact with partisan groups outside the ghetto. The book also describes a resistance appeal circulated shortly before the operation and a secret radio bulletin that carried news and encouragement. These are the book’s accounts of what people organized and remembered; they are not a complete inventory of every fighter or underground cell.

A separate USHMM article adds context about one organizer. It says Mordechai Tenenbaum came to Białystok from Warsaw in November 1942 to organize resistance and established a ghetto archive modeled on the Warsaw group Oneg Shabbat. That archive-building matters alongside armed preparation: documenting events was also a way of preserving evidence and affirming that Jewish life and history would not simply disappear. ([USHMM, “Spiritual Resistance in the Ghettos”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/spiritual-resistance-in-the-ghettos))

The memorial-book accounts describe the fighters as drawn from different political groups, a coalition forged under the pressure of Nazi persecution. Their practical problems were immense. Weapons were difficult to obtain; the book recalls smuggling, improvised explosives and grenades. It also remembers ties between the underground and forest partisans. The USHMM’s wider account of Jewish resistance across occupied Eastern Europe helps place Białystok in a regional pattern: in many ghettos, armed resistance aimed less at military victory than at disrupting deportations and escaping to partisan units. ([USHMM, “Jewish Uprisings in Ghettos and Camps, 1941–44”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-uprisings-in-ghettos-and-camps-1941-44))

## 16 August: fighting amid deportation

The memorial book’s accounts describe German forces entering the ghetto in the early hours of 16 August. One passage recalls fighters confronting them near Ciepła and Chmielna streets, under the leadership of Tenenbaum and Daniel Moszkowicz. In that account, the fighters attacked the gates in an attempt to open a route for Jews being driven toward the deportation point. A separate account describes setting buildings on fire during the fighting. The [Białystok ghetto resistance](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_12d70388b8ded08c15b9c173) was therefore both an armed revolt and an attempt to interrupt the roundup.

The two sources differ in emphasis and some details. One memorial-book account describes an initial battle lasting several hours and a group of about seventy fighters holding out in a bunker; another says major battles continued for several days, with resistance lingering into September. USHMM also describes five days of fighting, reports that seventy-one fighters were killed after capture in a bunker, and says more than a hundred people escaped to join partisan groups. These details are compatible with a revolt whose main fighting was crushed within days but whose consequences and scattered resistance continued afterward. They do not justify treating every reported number or duration as identical. ([USHMM, “Bialystok”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok))

The people named in the supplied records bring the scale of the tragedy back to individual lives. The book remembers [Lyube Subatnik](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_830668c467e28f8e213bb653), a track athlete who had married only months before the Holocaust, as falling in the uprising. The record ties her death specifically to 16 August. It also names [Fritz Gustav Fridl](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_7708e531d1e919761ed1834e) in connection with the August operation, describing him as a principal murderer in the ghetto passage. The available material here does not establish a fuller biography for either person, and the record about Fridl should not be expanded beyond what it supports.

The operation was not simply a battle between fighters and soldiers: it unfolded while the remaining ghetto population faced forced removal and death. The linked [Białystok ghetto](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_2fdfcf7a8cbf127724a57f47) was being destroyed as a community, and the uprising could not protect most people trapped inside. The USHMM account documents deportations to Treblinka and other camps, as well as the murder of children sent first to Theresienstadt and then Auschwitz-Birkenau. ([USHMM, “Bialystok”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok))

## Defeat, memory, and the unfinished record

The defeat was overwhelming, but the memorial book does not remember the revolt as meaningless. It describes fighters’ determination and their effort to make a path for others, while later commemorative accounts placed the dead in a shared community history. It recalls that the fighters’ remains were reburied in a mass grave after the war. Lyube Subatnik’s name is one reminder that remembrance must keep individual people visible, rather than reducing the uprising to a symbol alone.

The connected records also point toward questions that the uprising’s public story cannot answer by itself. The book names [the ghetto prison](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_11e607947c480fc3fd9b5061), [Praga Garden](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_d549fa75e74acf49c1211e32), and the [New World Synagogue](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_a37714960df70ec229762567) in accounts of wartime violence, but the supplied evidence does not establish their precise roles in the uprising. It also names Isaac Malmed, his wife and child, Milerzabludovsky, and Naftali Feldman with his wife among victims in related passages; the material provided does not show that these people took part in the August revolt. Their stories should not be folded into the uprising without further evidence.

The wider record confirms the central outline: the revolt began as the ghetto was being liquidated, aimed in part at escape toward the forests, and was defeated by overwhelming German force. The memorial book contributes something different and indispensable: the names, remembered preparations, street-level scenes, and the community’s judgment that resistance mattered even in defeat. Read together, these sources make the uprising neither a tale of victory nor merely a military episode. It was a desperate act of agency during the destruction of Białystok’s Jewish community—and a testimony that the people being deported were not passive participants in their own annihilation.
